headline: Rainbows are sunlight split into its hidden spectrum by millions of tiny prisms
universal_truth: White light contains all colors—what seems simple often holds hidden complexity
fun_facts: Every raindrop creates its own tiny rainbow—you see millions of them combined
You can never reach the 'end' of a rainbow because it moves as you move
There's always a fainter secondary rainbow above the main one, with colors reversed
discussion_questions: What hidden complexity exists in things you take for granted?
Why do you think rainbows appear in so many cultural myths and symbols?
What's something that seemed simple until you understood its depth?

hook.script: A rainbow isn't really there—not like a tree or a building. It's an optical phenomenon, a trick of light and geometry. Each raindrop is a tiny prism, bending sunlight and sending colors toward your eyes. Today, we unwrap this gift from physics.

cliff.script: Sunlight looks white. But Isaac Newton showed it contains all colors, hidden until something separates them. How does a raindrop split white light into red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet?

options.text: Light bends when entering and exiting the drop, separating colors by wavelength
options.response: Exactly. Each color bends at a slightly different angle—that's refraction.

options.text: Water naturally has rainbow-colored particles that light reveals
options.response: The colors actually come from the light itself...

fact1.title: Refraction and Reflection
fact1.script: Light enters a raindrop and bends—that's refraction. It reflects off the back of the drop and exits, bending again. Each color bends at a slightly different angle: red least, violet most. That's what fans white light into a spectrum.

fact2.title: Million Tiny Rainbows
fact2.script: Each raindrop creates its own complete rainbow. But you only see one color from each drop, depending on the angle. Millions of drops at different heights contribute different colors. The rainbow you see is a collaborative illusion.

fact3.title: The Hidden Double
fact3.script: Above every primary rainbow is a fainter secondary rainbow with colors reversed. It's created by light bouncing twice inside each raindrop. The space between them is darker than the sky around it—called Alexander's Dark Band.

wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: White light contains all colors. What appears simple—a beam of sunlight—holds hidden complexity. So do people, situations, and problems. Look deeper; there's always more than what first meets the eye.

outro.script: That's Day 41. Tomorrow, we'll discover why seasons change. Until then, next time you see a rainbow, look for its fainter twin above—and appreciate the physics painting the sky.

growTrack.title: Hidden Spectrum - Look Deeper
growTrack.learning_objective: Practice seeing complexity in seemingly simple things
growTrack.activity: Choose something 'simple' in your life—a relationship, a habit, a routine task. Spend 5 minutes exploring its hidden complexity. What 'colors' are hiding in the white light of the obvious?
